vignette: Worldwide searches for something, week by week, over three years. What were people looking for?
hints: Look at what happens every December, and on the day after the peak.
Climbs from early November, peaks in the week of 25 December, gone by mid-January. Not a deal, not a resolution.
explanation: Almost nothing for 10 months, a slow climb from early November, a peak in Christmas week, then a crash the moment it's over: searches for "Christmas songs" (the same shape as streams of a certain Mariah Carey track). Advent calendars peak in late November, Black Friday on one week in November, and New Year's resolutions in the first week of January. The tiny July blip is "Christmas in July". Values are approximate, drawn to match the Google Trends shape.
features: Near zero most of the year
Peak in the week of 25 December
pearl: A long ramp and a sharp cliff is the signature of a festive deadline. The steeper the cliff, the more people never want to hear it again.

vignette: Something measured once a day for two months. Name it.
hints: Count the days between peaks. About a month, isn't it? A fair few things repeat about monthly.
It goes right from 0% to 100% and back every 29½ days. Look up tonight.
explanation: A smooth wave from 0% to 100% and back, repeating every 29.5 days: the fraction of the Moon's face that's lit, from new moon (0%, 29 January 2025) to full moon (100%, 13 January and 12 February 2025). The Earth–Moon distance repeats every 27.6 days but never goes near zero; tides follow a two-week spring–neap cycle; day length changes over a year, not a month. Calculated from the lunar cycle, rounded to whole percent.
features: Full moon 13 Jan and 12 Feb; new moon 29 Jan
pearl: Period tells you the clock: 29.5 days is the Moon's phases, 27.6 its distance, 14.8 the spring–neap tides, 365 the Sun.

vignette: Average daily maximum temperature, month by month, for a famous city. Which one?
hints: No winter, no summer. What kind of place has that?
About 31 °C every month, with no midsummer monsoon dip. It's barely 1° from the equator, at sea level.
explanation: An almost flat line around 30–33 °C all year: Singapore, about 1° north of the equator. Mumbai looks similar but dips in July–August under monsoon cloud; Honolulu peaks in August and is cooler in January; Dubai swings from about 24 °C to over 40 °C. Quito is also on the equator, but it's 2,800 m up, so its highs sit near 19 °C. Lima has a clear cool season. Values are approximate long-term averages.
features: Range of only about 2 °C across the year
No dip for a monsoon or winter
pearl: Near the equator, height beats latitude: same sun, but every 1,000 m up costs about 6.5 °C.

vignette: A sum of money, in millions of Swedish kronor, set once a year since 1901. Today's a very good day to guess it.
options: A Swedish prime minister's yearly salary
The price of a new Volvo
hints: Nearly flat for 60 years, then up. A Volvo didn't exist in 1901, and Eurovision winners get a trophy, not a pay packet.
It was paid to Marie Curie, twice.
explanation: About 150,000 kronor in 1901, 10 million by 2001, a cut to 8 million in 2012 when the Foundation's investment returns slipped, and 11 million since 2023: the money for one full Nobel Prize, per the Nobel Foundation. It's shared when a prize is split. The line is not adjusted for inflation: in real terms the 1901 prize was worth more than you'd think, and the mid-century ones much less. Volvo started in 1927 and Eurovision pays no prize money at all.
features: The 2012 cut, then back up to 11 million
pearl: Alfred Nobel's will left the money to be invested and the interest paid out, so the prize is really a 125-year-old investment account with a very good mailing list.

vignette: The price of something in the United States, in US dollars, from 1986 to 2025. What is it?
hints: Check the y-axis: $1.60 to about $5.80. A smooth rise, no wild spikes. That rules out the volatile stuff.
The Economist has tracked this exact price since 1986 to compare currencies. Two all-beef patties...
explanation: From $1.60 in 1986 to about $5.80 in 2025: the US price of a Big Mac, used by The Economist's Big Mac Index since 1986 to compare currencies. A cinema ticket went from about $3.70 to over $11; a stamp from 22 to 78 cents; petrol and eggs jump around with crises rather than rising smoothly. Values are approximate and rounded.
pearl: Same burger, different price: the Big Mac Index shows whether a currency is over- or undervalued, one bun at a time.

vignette: A time of day, worked out for every day of 2025 in one Australian city. What's being timed?
hints: Two overnight jumps of exactly one hour. What changes clocks overnight, and which places do it?
On the clock it's latest (about 7:10) just before the April jump and earliest (about 5:30) just before the October one. Something that happens at the start of the day.
explanation: Sydney's sunrise, worked out for every day of 2025: about 5:50 on New Year's Day, drifting later to about 7:10 by early April, then jumping an hour earlier when daylight saving ended on 6 April. It's about 7:00 around the June solstice, then gets earlier through spring to about 5:30, until daylight saving starts on 5 October and pushes it an hour later. The earliest sunrise under daylight saving is about 5:37 in early December. Sunset would be latest in summer, not earliest; Perth and Brisbane don't use daylight saving, so no jumps; London's jumps fall in March and October the other way round, with sunrise latest in December.
features: Two one-hour jumps: early April and early October
Latest on the clock (about 7:10) just before the April jump
Earliest (about 5:30) just before the October jump
A second low of about 5:37 in early December
pearl: Daylight saving doesn't add any daylight: it just moves sunrise and sunset an hour later on the clock. The sun hasn't noticed.

vignette: An angle, measured once a day through 2025 in Sydney. What is it?
answer: How high the midday sun gets in Sydney
options: How high the midday sun gets in Sydney
The tilt of the Earth's axis
How high the midday sun gets in Darwin
hints: The axis is in degrees, and the line is a smooth yearly wave, lowest in June. What's highest in the sky in summer?
About 80 degrees at the December solstice, about 33 in June. In Darwin it would nearly reach straight overhead, twice a year.
explanation: The height of the sun above the horizon at midday in Sydney (about 34° S): close to 80° at the December solstice and about 33° at the June solstice, the difference being twice the Earth's 23.4° tilt. The tilt itself barely changes over a year. Darwin, inside the tropics, has the sun directly overhead twice a year, so its line would touch 90. Hours of daylight has the same shape, but it's measured in hours, not degrees.
features: Low point of about 33° in late June
High point of about 80° in late December
Gap between the two of about 47°: twice the Earth's tilt
pearl: Low winter sun is why your shadow at lunch in June is longer than you are, and why a north-facing window is gold in an Australian house.

vignette: A world record in seconds, as it stood at the end of each year since 1968 (as recognised today). Which record?
options: Fastest 0–100 km/h in a road car
hints: Just under 10 seconds, falling in hundredths. Which race is over in about that time?
Flat for 15 years from 1968, then small steps, then a huge drop in 2008–09 from one Jamaican sprinter.
explanation: The men's 100 m world record: Jim Hines' 9.95 in 1968 (the first electronically timed record under 10 seconds), then small steps from Carl Lewis, Leroy Burrell, Donovan Bailey, Maurice Greene and Asafa Powell, until Usain Bolt took it from 9.72 to 9.69 in 2008 and 9.58 in Berlin in 2009. Times later annulled for doping aren't shown. The women's record is 10.49, swimmers take about 47 seconds, and the 200 m is around 19.
features: Steps of a few hundredths through the 1990s
pearl: Bolt's 9.58 included a reaction time of 0.146 s: slower than several rivals out of the blocks, and still nobody has come close.

vignette: A world record in minutes, as it stood at the end of each year since 1990. Which record?
hints: Just over two hours, and it keeps creeping towards exactly two. Which race is that long?
Flat for a decade from 1988, then a run of Berlin and Chicago records. A Kenyan set it in 2023 and died in a road crash the next year.
explanation: The men's marathon world record: Belayneh Dinsamo's 2:06:50 (1988) stood for a decade, then Ronaldo da Costa, Khalid Khannouchi, Paul Tergat, Haile Gebrselassie, Patrick Makau, Wilson Kipsang, Dennis Kimetto and Eliud Kipchoge chipped it down, mostly in Berlin, until Kelvin Kiptum ran 2:00:35 in Chicago in 2023. The women's record is about 2:09–2:10, the half marathon under an hour, and race walkers take over 3½ hours for 50 km.
features: Lots of small cuts, mostly in Berlin
pearl: Kipchoge ran 1:59:40 in Vienna in 2019, but with rotating pacemakers and a laser guide car, so it never counted as a record.

vignette: A count, checked every five years since 1945. What's being counted?
answer: Member countries of the United Nations
options: Member countries of the United Nations
Stars on the European Union flag
Countries with the vote for women
hints: 51 at the start, in the year a famous world body was founded. Big jumps when colonies won independence, and again after the Soviet Union broke up.
Stuck at 193 since 2011, when South Sudan joined.
explanation: Member states of the United Nations: 51 founders in 1945, a surge in 1960 as 17 newly independent countries (16 of them African) joined, another after the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia broke up in the early 1990s, and 193 since South Sudan in 2011. FIFA has over 200 members and the Olympics have had over 200 teams; the EU flag has always had 12 stars; the Commonwealth has about 56.
features: A second jump in the early 1990s
pearl: Two places sit in the UN as observers, not members: the Holy See and Palestine.

vignette: The number of pages in each book of a seven-book series, by the year it came out (first UK editions). Which series?
options: A Song of Ice and Fire
hints: Seven books, from 1997 to 2007, each one getting much longer. Narnia also has seven, but they're all short and came out in the 1950s.
Book five is the longest at well over 700 pages. The last two are exactly the same length.
explanation: First UK editions of the Harry Potter books: Philosopher's Stone 223 pages (1997), then 251, 317, a leap to 636 for Goblet of Fire (2000), a peak of 766 for Order of the Phoenix (2003), and 607 each for Half-Blood Prince and Deathly Hallows. Narnia's seven books are all about 200 pages and appeared in the 1950s; A Song of Ice and Fire has five books so far; Hunger Games, Twilight and Percy Jackson have fewer books.
features: Last two exactly the same length
pearl: Readers waited three years between books four and five, and the reward was the longest one. Page counts vary by edition: US hardbacks are longer because of bigger type.

vignette: A running total of something, at the end of each year since 1996. What's being counted?
options: Stars on the Hollywood Walk of Fame
hints: 151 to start, in 1996. A new batch every few years, each time a new pair of games comes out.
Gotta catch them all: over 1,000 by 2022.
explanation: The total number of Pokémon species: 151 in the original 1996 Red and Green games, then a jump with every new generation of games (251, 386, 493, 649, 721, 809, 898) to 1,025 by 2024. Emoji also arrive in yearly batches, but there are thousands; Lego sets number in the tens of thousands; Smash Bros. has under 100 fighters.
features: A staircase, one step per new generation of games
pearl: Pokémon number 1 in the National Pokédex is Bulbasaur, but the first one ever designed is said to be Rhydon.

vignette: A height in metres, as it stood at the end of each year since 1930. What's being measured?
options: The world's tallest structure of any kind
The deepest a person has dived
hints: New York held it for decades: first 319 m, then 381 m from 1931. Then Chicago, Kuala Lumpur and Taipei.
Since 2010, Dubai, at 828 m.
explanation: The height of the world's tallest building: the Chrysler Building (319 m, 1930), the Empire State Building (381 m, 1931) for over 40 years, the World Trade Center (417 m) and Sears Tower (442 m) in the early 1970s, the Petronas Towers (452 m, 1998), Taipei 101 (508 m, 2004) and the Burj Khalifa (828 m) since 2010. Radio masts made the tallest structure taller than the tallest building for decades; Australia's tallest building is about 323 m (Q1, Gold Coast).
features: A huge jump to 828 m in 2010
pearl: The Burj Khalifa's top floors are so high that you can watch the sun set from the ground, take a fast lift up and watch it set again.

vignette: The number of teams at a famous sports tournament, each time it's held, since 1930. Which tournament?
hints: Started in 1930, every four years, with a gap for the Second World War.
16 teams for decades, then 24, then 32, and 48 in North America in 2026.
explanation: Teams at the men's FIFA World Cup: 13 at the first one in Uruguay in 1930, no tournaments in 1942 or 1946, 16 teams from 1954 to 1978, 24 from 1982, 32 from 1998, and 48 at the 2026 World Cup in the US, Canada and Mexico. The Women's World Cup started in 1991, the Rugby World Cup in 1987, the Cricket World Cup in 1975, and the Euros have never had more than 24.
pearl: Only 13 teams went to the 1930 World Cup because most of Europe didn't fancy a three-week boat trip to Uruguay.

vignette: A running total, at the end of each year since 1972. Every step is exactly one. What's being counted?
answer: Leap seconds added to the world's clocks
options: Leap seconds added to the world's clocks
Changes to Australian daylight saving rules
Total solar eclipses seen from Australia
Countries that joined the European Union
hints: Leap days would go up every four years like clockwork. This is irregular, because it follows the Earth, not the calendar.
Clocks got an extra second at midnight UTC on 30 June or 31 December. 27 in all, none since 2016.
explanation: Leap seconds: an extra second added to UTC at the end of 30 June or 31 December when the Earth's spin fell far enough behind atomic clocks. There were 2 in 1972 and one most years in the 1970s, then they came less often, with the last on 31 December 2016: 27 in all. Leap days are regular (every four years); there were six crewed Moon landings, all before 1973.
features: Two in 1972, then about one a year through the 1970s
pearl: In 2022 the world's timekeepers voted to scrap leap seconds by 2035. Lately the Earth has been spinning slightly faster, so the next one might have had to be taken away.
